objectives: Recognise wh as a two-letter grapheme at the start of taught words.
Read wh-words such as when, whip, whiz and wham using the common /w/ pronunciation.
Notice that wh and w often represent the same sound in many English accents.
Learn that some words, including who, are exceptions and will be taught separately.
concepts: A grapheme is a written letter or group of letters representing a sound.
In many English accents, wh and w are pronounced alike in words such as when and win.
The spelling pattern can be identified visually even when the sound matches w.
English spelling has exceptions; do not assume every wh-word follows one rule.

definitions.definition: A letter or group of letters used to represent a sound.
A recurring written pattern in words.
A word that does not follow the pattern being studied.

workedExamples.solution: The word begins with the two-letter grapheme wh; in many accents it starts with /w/.
The initial wh represents the same /w/ sound heard at the start of win in many accents.
This is an exception: wh is pronounced /h/; it will be taught as a special word.

commonMistakes: Claiming wh and w always make different sounds.
Assuming every wh-word is pronounced the same way.
Forgetting that accents differ and who is an exception.
keyTakeaways: Recognise wh as a two-letter initial grapheme.
In common taught words, pronounce wh as /w/ in many accents.
Use spelling to identify the pattern even when the sound matches w.

activities.name: Identify wh at the beginning of printed words and compare with w.
steps: Highlight wh in taught printed words.
Read the whole word aloud in the learner's accent.
Compare the spelling with a w-word that shares the common /w/ sound.
Note who as a special word for separate teaching.
